summary: Gives an algorithmic description of how an RSVP implementation processes messages. It is meant to clarify the version 1 specification in RFC 2205 and help implementers build programs that behave the same way. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2209 gives algorithmic rules for processing RSVP version 1 messages. It explains what state implementations keep and how messages change path and reservation information.

questions: how do rsvp refresh messages work
subtitle: Algorithmic rules for how RSVP version 1 implementations process messages and state.

tldr.problem: The RSVP version 1 specification needs implementation rules that explain how hosts and routers process messages and maintain reservation state.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2209 describes message-processing sequences and four state blocks used for paths, reservations, traffic control and admission-control failures.
tldr.outcome: This Informational memo clarifies processing for the RSVP protocol defined in RFC 2205; it does not specify an Internet standard.

today: RFC 2209 is an Informational memo published in September 1997, and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes processing rules for the RSVP version 1 specification in RFC 2205.

sections.title: Purpose of the Processing Rules
sections.content:
RFC 2209 provides a generic algorithmic description of how an RSVP implementation processes messages. It is intended to clarify the version 1 RSVP specification in RFC 2205, and deliberately omits some implementation details.

The memo assumes generic interface calls and identifies information that implementations need to maintain. An implementation may use additional or different internal data structures, provided its operation follows the described rules.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo explains the steps an RSVP implementation follows when messages arrive. It clarifies the protocol rules without requiring one specific internal software design.

sections.title: Four RSVP State Blocks
sections.content:
A Path State Block (PSB) stores path information for a session and sender, including the sender traffic specification and previous hop. A Reservation State Block (RSB) stores a reservation request, its next hop, filter information, style and flowspec. These blocks let an implementation match reservations with paths.

A Traffic Control State Block (TCSB) records reservation information passed to traffic control for an outgoing interface. A Blockade State Block (BSB) records an admission-control failure and related timer state. The RFC describes these as generic structures; implementations may organize their data differently.
sections.plainLanguage: RSVP keeps separate records for sender paths, reservation requests, reservations installed at an interface and failed admission attempts. The records help the implementation match requests to the right traffic.

sections.title: Checking and Processing Messages
sections.content:
When a message arrives, the implementation checks the RSVP version and checksum, parses required objects, and verifies an INTEGRITY object if one is present. It forwards messages not addressed to a local interface, except for the message types that the rules require the router to process locally. Invalid messages are discarded.

A PATH message creates or updates path state and may trigger path and reservation refreshes. A RESV message checks for matching path state and compatible reservation styles, then creates or updates reservation state. PTEAR and RTEAR messages remove path or reservation state; PERR and RERR messages report errors along the relevant path.
sections.plainLanguage: RSVP first checks whether a message is valid and belongs at the current router. It then updates path or reservation records, removes state when asked, or forwards error information.

sections.title: Applying Reservation Changes
sections.content:
When path or reservation state changes, the implementation updates the local traffic-control system to match. It combines matching reservation flowspecs and filter specifications for an outgoing interface, then creates, modifies or deletes the corresponding traffic-control state.

If the traffic-control operation fails, the rules describe sending a reservation error and handling the affected reservation state. A change can also cause an RSVP event notification to local applications and a reservation refresh toward the previous hop.
sections.plainLanguage: When a reservation changes, the router updates the traffic-control settings for the outgoing interface. It can notify applications and send refreshed reservation information to the previous hop.

sections.title: Refreshing Paths and Reservations
sections.content:
PATH refreshes carry sender and path information downstream. The implementation sends copies on the outgoing interfaces for the path, updates the time-to-live value and supplies interface information in the RSVP_HOP object. If the resulting time-to-live is zero, it does not send the PATH message.

RESV refreshes travel toward previous hops. The implementation finds matching reservations, merges flowspec and filter information according to reservation style, and builds a RESV message. These procedures allow RSVP state to be refreshed after message loss or router restart.
sections.plainLanguage: PATH refreshes carry sender information downstream, and RESV refreshes carry reservation information upstream. The RFC specifies how each message is rebuilt from the state kept by the router.
